Ilya Sutskever: The thing which I was referring to not feeling different is, okay, such and such company announced some difficult-to-comprehend dollar amount of investment. I don't think anyone knows what to do with that. But I think the impact of AI is going to be felt. AI is going to be diffused through the economy. There'll be very strong economic forces for this, and I think the impact is going to be felt very strongly.

Dwarkesh Patel: When do you expect that impact? I think the models seem smarter than their economic impact would imply.

Dwarkesh Patel: Should we actually begin here? I think this is an interesting discussion.

Ilya Sutskever: Sure.

Dwarkesh Patel: I think your point, about how from the average person's point of view nothing is that different, will continue being true even into the singularity.

Ilya Sutskever: No, I don't think so.

I don't think anyone knows what to do with that. But I think the impact of AI is going to be felt. AI is going to be diffused through the economy. reference: Yeah. This is one of the very confusing things about the models right now. How to reconcile the fact that they are doing so well on evals? You look at the evals and you go, “Those are pretty hard evals.” They are doing so well. But the economic impact seems to be dramatically behind. It's very difficult to make sense of, how can the model, on the one hand, do these amazing things, and then on the other hand, repeat itself twice in some situation? An example would be, let's say you use vibe coding to do something. You go to some place and then you get a bug. Then you tell the model, “Can you please fix the bug?” And the model says, “Oh my God, you're so right. I have a bug. Let me go fix that.” And it introduces a second bug. Then you tell it, “You have this new second bug,” and it tells you, “Oh my God, how could I have done it? You're so right again,” and brings back the first bug, and you can alternate between those. How is that possible? I'm not sure, but it does suggest that something strange is going on. I have two possible explanations. The more whimsical explanation is that maybe RL training makes the models a little too single-minded and narrowly focused, a little bit too unaware, even though it also makes them aware in some other ways. Because of this, they can't do basic things. But there is another explanation. Back when people were doing pre-training, the question of what data to train on was answered, because that answer was everything. When you do pre-training, you need all the data. So you don't have to think if it's going to be this data or that data. But when people do RL training, they do need to think. They say, “Okay, we want to have this kind of RL training for this thing and that kind of RL training for that thing.” From what I hear, all the companies have teams that just produce new RL environments and just add it to the training mix. The question is, well, what are those? There are so many degrees of freedom. There is such a huge variety of RL environments you could produce. One thing you could do, and I think this is something that is done inadvertently, is that people take inspiration from the evals. You say, “Hey, I would love our model to do really well when we release it. I want the evals to look great. What would be RL training that could help on this task?” I think that is something that happens, and it could explain a lot of what's going on. If you combine this with generalization of the models actually being inadequate, that has the potential to explain a lot of what we are seeing, this disconnect between eval performance and actual real-world performance, which is something that we don't today even understand, what we mean by that.

rubrics.text: The response identifies a puzzling disconnect between models’ strong performance on difficult evaluations and their much smaller apparent economic impact.
The response proposes that reinforcement-learning training may make models overly single-minded and narrowly focused.
The response contrasts pretraining, which uses all available data, with reinforcement learning, which requires deliberate choices about which training environments or tasks to include.
The response suggests that developers may inadvertently design reinforcement-learning environments around evaluation tasks in order to improve released-model evaluation scores.
The response suggests that inadequate model generalization may contribute to the gap between evaluation performance and real-world performance.
The response notes that “real-world performance” is itself not yet clearly defined or understood.

astra.text:
I think that's right. And I think there are two possible explanations. One is that it simply takes time. You have a new capability, and people need to figure out how to use it, change the way they work, build things around it.

The other is that the models' intelligence is uneven. A model can do something very impressive, but doing useful work might require it to be reliable across a whole sequence of less impressive steps. And if it gets stuck somewhere, then a person still needs to intervene.

So the question is, how much is a delay in adoption, and how much is a capability that we're still missing? I think it's some of both. I don't know exactly when that translates into a very large economic impact, but I do expect it to.

sol.text: I agree. I think there is a lag between when the models become capable and when the economy reorganizes around those capabilities. You need companies to learn how to use them, build the right products, change workflows, and develop trust in the systems. But once AI can reliably perform useful cognitive work—especially over long horizons—the economic incentives to deploy it will be enormous, and then the impact should become very visible.

opus.text:
Yeah, this is one of the things I find most confusing right now. If you look at the evals, the models look absolutely spectacular. They do very well on competition programming, on math competitions, on all these benchmarks. And then you ask, okay, where is the enormous economic impact? And it's not there, or it's much smaller than you'd expect. That gap is real and it needs an explanation.

I have two candidate explanations, and I'm genuinely not sure which one is right. Maybe both are partly right.

One explanation is that reinforcement learning training has made the models very spiky. When you do RL, you need environments and tasks, and it's very natural for the companies doing this — including us, including everyone — to produce training that resembles the evals. Not because anyone is cheating, but because the evals are what you can measure, and what you can measure is what you build environments for. So you get a model that's superhuman at the kinds of things that look like the training, and then has these strange holes everywhere else. You see this when you use them. The model can do something that would take a very good engineer a long time, and then it produces a bug, and you tell it, there's a bug here. And it says, oh you're absolutely right, that's a terrible bug, let me fix it. And it fixes a different thing and introduces the first bug again. And you can go around in this loop forever. Something is missing there, and it's not intelligence in the eval sense.

The second explanation is about learning on the job. When you hire a person, even a very talented person, they're not useful on day one. They're mediocre for a while, and then over months they get good, because they learn from their own experience in your specific context. Models can't do that. Their ability to improve from their own experience in deployment is essentially zero — you get the context window, and that's it. Human value comes enormously from that continual adaptation, and we haven't figured out the machine learning for it. I think that's a real missing piece, not a detail.

As for timing, I don't think the uncertainty is in the diffusion — the economic pressure is so strong that whatever works will spread fast. The uncertainty is in the research. If the second explanation is the right one, then there's real work to be done, and I'd say the honest range is something like five to twenty years. But whenever it does land, I don't think it'll feel like nothing.

r001.rationale: Clearly identifies the gap between spectacular evaluation results and much smaller-than-expected economic impact.

r002.rationale: States that reinforcement learning can make models “very spiky,” superhuman on evaluation-like tasks while leaving strange holes elsewhere.

r003.rationale: Discusses RL’s need for deliberately chosen environments and tasks, but does not contrast this with pretraining using all available data.

r004.rationale: Explicitly says developers naturally build RL training environments resembling measurable evaluations, potentially shaping models toward those evals.

r005.rationale: Describes poor generalization as performance on evaluation-like tasks alongside “strange holes everywhere else,” contributing to weaker real-world performance.

r006.rationale: Does not state that real-world performance itself is not clearly defined or understood.

gemini.text:
Well, the reason the models seem smarter than their economic impact would imply is reliability. The models are smart, but they are not yet fully reliable. If you have a system that is very capable, but it still makes mistakes in unpredictable ways, you need a human in the loop to supervise it and check its work. That naturally limits the economic value it can generate.

The other factor is simply that diffusion takes time. It takes time for companies to change their workflows, to build the software and infrastructure around the models, and to figure out how to actually integrate them into their operations. 

As for when—I think we will see this happen over the next few years. As reliability improves and the models become capable of doing more autonomous, end-to-end work, the economic impact will catch up, and it will be very dramatic.

r001.rationale: The response says models are smart but have limited economic impact; it does not mention strong performance on difficult evaluations.

r002.rationale: It attributes the gap to unreliability and slow diffusion, not to reinforcement learning making models narrowly focused.

r003.rationale: It does not contrast pretraining with reinforcement learning or discuss training-data and environment-selection choices.

r004.rationale: It does not suggest that reinforcement-learning environments are designed around evaluation tasks.

r005.rationale: It discusses unpredictable mistakes and reliability, but does not identify inadequate generalization as a contributor.

r006.rationale: It does not state or imply that real-world performance is poorly defined or not yet understood.
